'''''Ulmus glabra''''', the '''wych elm''' or '''Scots elm''', has the widest range of the European elm species, from Ireland eastwards to the [[Ural Mountains]], and from the [[Arctic Circle]] south to the mountains of the [[Peloponnese]] and [[Sicily]], where the species reaches its southern limit in Europe;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Raimondo |first=Francesco Maria |date=1 January 1977 |title=First finding of ''Ulmus glabra'' Huds. on the Madonie, Northern Sicily |journal=Webbia |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=261–277 |doi=10.1080/00837792.1977.10670074 |issn=0083-7792 |doi-access=free }}</ref> it is also native to the Caucasus region and parts of Western Asia (Turkey, Syria and Iran).<ref name=POWO/> A large [[deciduous]] tree, it is essentially a [[montane]] species, growing at altitudes up to {{convert|1500|m|ft|-3|abbr=on}}, preferring sites with moist soils and high humidity.<ref name="Heybroek,1">Heybroek, H. M., Goudzwaard, L, Kaljee, H. (2009). ''Iep of olm, karakterboom van de Lage Landen'' (:Elm, a tree with character of the Low Countries). KNNV, Uitgeverij. {{ISBN|9789050112819 }}</ref> The tree can form pure forests in [[Scandinavia]] and occurs as far north as latitude [[67th parallel north|67°N]] at [[Beiarn Municipality]] in Norway. It has been successfully introduced as far north as [[Tromsø (city)|Tromsø]] and [[Alta (town)|Alta]] in northern Norway ([[70th parallel north|70°N]]).<ref>{{Cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926114351/https://www.nhm.uio.no/besok-oss/botanisk-hage/avdelinger/arboretet/trar/alm/utbredelse/ |title=Utbredelse - Naturhistorisk museum |url=https://www.nhm.uio.no/besok-oss/botanisk-hage/avdelinger/arboretet/trar/alm/utbredelse/ |archive-date=26 September 2020 }}</ref> It has also been successfully introduced to [[Narsarsuaq]], near the southern tip of Greenland ([[61st parallel north|61°N]]).

The tree was by far the most common elm in the north and west of the [[British Isles]] and is now acknowledged as the only indisputably British native elm species. Owing to its former abundance in Scotland, the tree was occasionally (primarily historically) known as Scots elm; [[Loch Lomond]] is said to be derived from the [[Scottish Gaelic|Gaelic]] {{Lang|gd|Lac Leaman}}, interpreted by some as 'Lake of the Elms', 'leaman' being the genitive plural form of leam or lem, 'elm'.<ref name=Richens>Richens, R. H. (1983). ''Elm''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521294621}}</ref>

Closely related species, such as Bergmann's elm, ''[[Ulmus bergmanniana|U. bergmanniana]]'', and the Manchurian elm, ''[[Ulmus laciniata|U. laciniata]]'', native to northeast Asia, were once sometimes included in ''U. glabra'';<ref name=Elwes>Elwes, H. J. & Henry, A. (1913). ''[https://web.archive.org/web/20080529055841/http://fax.libs.uga.edu/QK488xE4/1f/trees_of_britain_and_ireland_vol_7.pdf The Trees of Great Britain & Ireland]''. Vol. VII. 1848–1929. Republished 2014 Cambridge University Press, {{ISBN|9781108069380 }}</ref> another close relative is the Himalayan or Kashmir elm, ''[[Ulmus wallichiana|U. wallichiana]]''. Conversely, ''[[Ulmus elliptica|U. elliptica]]'' from the [[Caucasus]], considered a species by many authorities,<ref>{{cite web |title=''Ulmus elliptica'' K.Koch |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:856849-1 |access-date=2025-06-10}}</ref><ref>Elwes, Henry John, & Henry, Augustine, (1913) ''The Trees of Great Britain & Ireland'', Vol.7, pp.1863-1864 [https://archive.org/stream/treesofgreatbrit07elweuoft#page/1863/mode/2up]</ref><ref>Bean, W. J. (1988) ''Trees and shrubs hardy in Great Britain'', 8th edition, Murray, London</ref><ref>Krüssman, Gerd, ''Manual of Cultivated Broad-Leaved Trees & Shrubs'' (1984 vol. 3)</ref> is sometimes listed as a regional form of ''U. glabra''.<ref>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge 1983), p.279</ref>

==Etymology==
The word "wych" (also spelled "witch") comes from the Old English {{wikt-lang|ang|wice}}, meaning pliant or supple, which also gives definition to [[wicker]] and [[wikt:weak|weak]]. [[Jacob George Strutt]]'s 1822 book, ''Sylva Britannica'', attests that the wych elm was sometimes referred to as "wych hazel", a name now applied to the unrelated genus ''[[Hamamelis]]'', commonly called "wych hazels".<ref>{{cite book |title=Sylva Britannica |author=Jacob George Strutt |year=1822 |page=66}} [https://archive.org/stream/sylvabritannicao00strurich Full text] of expanded 1830 edition.</ref>

==Classification==

===Subspecies===
Some botanists, notably Lindquist (1931), have proposed two [[subspecies]]:<ref name="botexc1931v9p785">{{cite journal |last1=Bertil |first1=Lindguist |title=Two varieties of North West European Ulmus glabra |journal=Botanical Society Report |date=1931 |volume=9 |page=785 |url=https://archive.org/stream/reportbotanicals9192bota#page/785/mode/2up/ |access-date=29 August 2017 }}</ref>
* ''U. glabra'' subsp. ''glabra'' in the south of the species' range: broad leaves with short tapering base and acute lobes;<ref name="Myking&Yakovlev"/> trees often with a short, forked trunk and a low, broad crown;
* ''U. glabra'' subsp. ''montana'' <small>(Stokes) Lindqvist</small> in the north of the species' range (northern Britain, Scandinavia): leaves narrower, with a long tapering base and without acute lobes;<ref name="Myking&Yakovlev">{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/02827580500539265 |title=Variation in leaf morphology and chloroplast DNA in ''Ulmus glabra'' in the northern suture zone: Effects of distinct glacial refugia |year=2006 |last1=Myking |first1=Tor |last2=Yakovlev |first2=Igor |journal=Scandinavian Journal of Forest Research |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=99–107 |bibcode=2006SJFR...21...99M |s2cid=84736722 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233231433 }}</ref> trees commonly with a long single trunk and a tall, narrow crown.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20171109022903/http://bioportal.naturalis.nl/nba/result?nba_request=http%253A%252F%252Fapi.biodiversitydata.nl%252Fv0%252F%252Fmultimedia%252Fget-multimedia-object-for-specimen-within-result-set%252F%253FunitID%253DL.1587168_802534720%2526searchID%253Db8d223826c5c3693e0505034d8ec4229 bioportal.naturalis.nl L.1587168 ''Ulmus glabra'' Huds. subsp. ''montana'' (Stokes) Lindq., Thirsk, Yorkshire, 1937]</ref>

Much overlap is seen between populations with these characters, and the distinction may owe to environmental influence, rather than genetic variation; the subspecies are not accepted by either ''Flora Europaea'' or ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''.<ref name=Flora>[http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Ulmus&SPECIES_XREF=glabra&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= Flora Europaea: ''Ulmus glabra'']</ref><ref name=POWO/>

==Description==
The type sometimes reaches heights of {{convert|40|m|ft|abbr=on}}, typically with a broad crown where open-grown, supported by a short [[Bole (botany)|bole]] up to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} [[diameter at breast height]] (DBH). Normally, root suckers are not seen; natural reproduction is by seed alone. The tree is notable for its very tough, supple young shoots, which are always without the corky ridges or 'wings' characteristic of many elms. The alternate leaves are deciduous, {{Convert abbreviated|6-17|cm}} long by {{Convert abbreviated|3-12|cm}} broad, usually [[leaf shape|obovate]] with an asymmetric base, the lobe often completely covering the short (<5 mm) [[petiole (botany)|petiole]];<ref>{{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824735 }} Sheet labelled ''Ulmus scabra'' <small>Mill.</small> = ''Ulmus montana'' <small>[[William Withering|With.]]</small>; {{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824732 }} Sheet labelled ''Ulmus montana'' = ''Ulmus glabra'' <small>Huds.</small> RBGE specimen, 1900; {{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824730 }} Sheet described as ''Ulmus glabra'' <small>Huds.</small> from [[Bridge of Allan]], Scotland, 1899; {{Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh |id=E00824764 }} [[Cotyledon]] and seedling leaves, ''Ulmus scabra'' <small>Mill.</small> = ''Ulmus montana'' <small>[[William Withering|With.]]</small></ref> the upper surface is rough. Leaves on juvenile or shade-grown shoots sometimes have three or more lobes near the apex.<ref name=Coleman>Coleman, M (ed.). (2009). ''Wych Elm''. Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. {{ISBN|978-1-906129-21-7}}.</ref> The [[perfect flower|perfect]] [[plant sexuality|hermaphrodite]] [[flower]]s appear before the leaves in early spring, produced in clusters of 10–20; they are 4 mm across on 10 mm long stems, and being wind-pollinated, are [[apetalous]]. The fruit is a winged [[Samara (fruit)|samara]] 20 mm long and 15 mm broad, with a single, round, 6 mm seed in the centre, maturing in late spring.<ref name=Bean>Bean, W. J. (1981). ''Trees and shrubs hardy in Great Britain'', 7th edition. Murray, London.</ref><ref name=White>White, J. & More, D. (2003). ''Trees of Britain and Northern Europe''. Cassell's, London</ref> The roots can be of extraordinary length: one at Auchencraig, Larg, Ayershire, Scotland has roots which have been traced for a length of 110 metres from the trunk.<ref>{{cite book | last= McFarlan | first= Donald | last2= McWhirter | first2= Norris | date= 1990 | title= Guinness Book of Records - 1991 | location= London | publisher=Guinness Publishing Ltd.| page= 49}}</ref>

==Pests and diseases==
While the species is highly susceptible to [[Dutch elm disease]] (DED),<ref name=Forestry>[https://web.archive.org/web/20170309060523/https://www.forestry.gov.uk/fr/hcou-4u4jcl Forestry Commission. ''Dutch elm disease in Britain'', UK]</ref><ref name=Brasier>Brasier, C. M. (1996). [https://web.archive.org/web/20170706141305/https://www.forestry.gov.uk/pdf/New_horizons_DED.pdf/$FILE/New_horizons_DED.pdf New horizons in Dutch elm disease control]. Pages 20–28 in: ''Report on Forest Research'', 1996. Forestry Commission. HMSO, London, UK.</ref> it is less favoured as a host by the elm bark beetles, which act as vectors. Research in Spain has indicated the presence of a [[triterpene]], [[alnulin]], rendering the tree bark less attractive to the beetle than the [[Ulmus minor|field elm]], though at 87 μg/g dried bark, its concentration is not as effective as in ''[[Ulmus laevis]]'' (200 μg/g).<ref name="Martín">{{cite journal |doi=10.1139/x04-158 |title=Triterpenes in elms in Spain |year=2005 |last1=Martín-Benito |first1=Dario |last2=García-Vallejo |first2=Maria Concepción |last3=Pajares |first3=Juan Alberto |last4=López |first4=David |journal=Canadian Journal of Forest Research |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=199–205 |bibcode=2005CaJFR..35..199M |s2cid=85380172 |url=http://pubs.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/rp/rppdf/x04-158.pdf |access-date=18 June 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070628155809/http://pubs.nrc-cnrc.gc.ca/rp/rppdf/x04-158.pdf |archive-date=28 June 2007 }}</ref> Moreover, once the tree is dying, its bark is quickly colonized by the [[fungus]] ''[[Phoma]]'', which radically reduces the amount of bark available for the beetle to breed on.<ref name=Webber>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/292449a0 |title=A natural biological control of Dutch elm disease |year=1981 |last1=Webber |first1=Joan |journal=Nature |volume=292 |issue=5822 |pages=449–451 |bibcode=1981Natur.292..449W |s2cid=4328001 }}</ref> In European trials, clones of apparently resistant trees were inoculated with the pathogen, causing 85 – 100% wilting, resulting in 68% mortality by the following year. DNA analysis by [[Cemagref]] (now [[Irstea]]) in France has determined the genetic diversity within the species is very limited, making the chances of a resistant tree evolving rather remote.<ref name=Solla>Solla et al. (2005). [https://academic.oup.com/forestscience/article/51/2/134/4617585 "Screening European Elms for Resistance to Ophiostoma novo-ulmi".] ''Forest Science'', 134–141. 51 (2) 2005. Society of American Foresters.</ref>

A 300-year-old example growing in [[Grenzhammer]], [[Ilmenau]] has allegedly been scientifically proven to be resistant to Dutch elm disease.<ref>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701224339/https://www.thueringer-allgemeine.de/regionen/ilmenau/in-ilmenau-steht-die-einzige-resistente-bergulme-europas-id219949157.html?service=amp |title=In Ilmenau steht die einzige resistente Bergulme Europas |date=15 March 2014 |url=https://www.thueringer-allgemeine.de/regionen/ilmenau/in-ilmenau-steht-die-einzige-resistente-bergulme-europas-id219949157.html?service=amp |archive-date=1 July 2022 }}</ref> In 1998, over 700 healthy, mature trees were discovered on the upper slopes of Mount Šimonka in the [[Slanské Hills]] in [[Slovakia]],<ref>[https://www.vranovske.sk/bresty-zo-simonky-nechal-vysadit-v-kralovskom-sidle-aj-princ-charles/ Igor Kňazovický, 'Prince Charles had elms from Šimonka planted in the royal residence', Regional Tourism Organization, Horný Zemplín and Horný Šariš; 23 June 2020]</ref> where they are believed to have survived courtesy of their isolation from disease-carrying beetles rather than through any innate resistance; 50 clones of these trees, propagated by the Faculty of Forestry at the [[Technical University in Zvolen]], were presented to the Prince of Wales (now King [[Charles III]]) during his state visit in 1995 and planted at his [[Highgrove Estate]], in the [[Duchy of Cornwall]] estate, and at [[Clapham, North Yorkshire|Clapham]], [[Yorkshire]], in 2001.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ecosystems.sk/pages/news41.html |title=CST Slovakia - News |access-date=4 August 2006 |archive-date=16 September 2005 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050916201734/http://www.ecosystems.sk/pages/news41.html }}</ref> They remain disease-free (2024),<ref>Geraint Richards, 'All the King's Elms: re-elming the Duchy of Cornwall estate', in Mark Seddon and David Shreeve, eds., ''Great British Elms'' (Kew Gardens, 2024), p.181</ref><ref>[https://lf.tuzvo.sk/sk/timova-spolupraca-za-uspesnym-pribehom-slovenskych-brestov-v-kralovskych-zahradach-v-highgrove Miroslava Babiaková, 'Teamwork behind the success story of Slovak elms in the royal gardens at Highgrove'; Faculty of Forestry, Technical University of Svolen, Slovakia, 31 October 2019; lf.tuzvo.sk]</ref><ref>Andrej Barát, 'Les princa Charlesa zdobia slovenské bresty. Už 20 rokov' [: Prince Charles' Estate has been adorned with Slovak elms for 20 years], 13 February 2020, zurnal.pravda.sk</ref> however, the specimen donated by the Prince in 2004 to Butterfly Conservation's trial plantation at Great Fontley, Hampshire, succumbed to DED in 2020.<ref name="Brookes">Brookes, A. H. (2025). ''Great Fontley Elm Trial, 2025 Report''. Butterfly Conservation, Lulworth, England.</ref>

The Swedish Forest Tree Breeding Association at [[Källstorp]] produced [[triploid]] and [[tetraploid]] forms of the tree, but these proved no more resistant to Dutch elm disease than the normal [[diploid]] form.<ref name=Went>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/BF02151105 |title=The Dutch elm disease - Summary of fifteen years hybridisation and selection work (1937–1952) |year=1954 |last1=Went |first1=Johanna C. |journal=European Journal of Plant Pathology |volume=60 |issue=2 |pages=109–127 |bibcode=1954EJPP...60..109W |s2cid=38868071 }}</ref>

In trials conducted in Italy, the tree was found to have a slight to moderate susceptibility to [[Elm Yellows|elm yellows]], and a high susceptibility to the elm leaf beetle ''[[Xanthogaleruca luteola]]''.<ref name=Mittempergher>{{cite journal |last1=Mittempergher |first1=L |last2=Santini |first2=A |journal=Investigacion Agraria: Sistemas y Recursos Forestales |title=The history of elm breeding |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=161–177 |date=2004 |url=http://www.inia.es/gcontrec/Pub/161-177-(14)-The_history_1161943529015.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211155148/http://www.inia.es/gcontrec/Pub/161-177-(14)-The_history_1161943529015.pdf |archive-date=11 February 2017 }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
The wych elm is moderately shade-tolerant, but requires deep, rich soils as typically found along river valleys.<ref name=Edlin>Edlin, H. L. (1949). ''British woodland trees''. Batsford, London.</ref> The species is intolerant of acid soils and flooding,<ref name=Thomas>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/1365-2745.12994 |title=Biological Flora of the British Isles: ''Ulmus glabra'' |year=2018 |last1=Thomas |first1=Peter A. |last2=Stone |first2=Duncan |last3=La Porta |first3=Nicola |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=106 |issue=4 |pages=1724–1766 |bibcode=2018JEcol.106.1724T |s2cid=89800637 |url=https://openpub.fmach.it/retrieve/handle/10449/49595/77476/2018%20Thomas%20et%20al%20-%20Ulmus%20glabra%20-%20J-Ecol.pdf }}</ref> as it is of prolonged drought.<ref name=CAB>CAB International (2005) ''Forestry Compendium''. CAB International, Wallingford, UK</ref> Although rarely used as a street tree owing to its shape, it can be surprisingly tolerant of urban air pollution, constricted growing conditions, and severe pollarding.

As wych elm does not sucker from the roots, and any seedlings are often consumed by uncontrolled deer populations, regeneration is very restricted, limited to sprouts from the stumps of young trees. The resultant decline has been extreme, and the wych elm is now uncommon over much of its former range. It is best propagated from seed or by layering stooled stock plants, although softwood cuttings taken in early June will root fairly reliably under mist.<ref name=Beckett>Beckett, K. & G. (1979). ''Planting Native Trees and Shrubs''. Jarrold & Sons, Norwich, UK.</ref>

Wych elm was widely planted in Edinburgh in the 19th century as a park and avenue tree, and despite losses, it remains abundant there, regenerating through seedlings.<ref>Coleman, Max, ed., ''Wych Elm'' (Edinburgh, 2009)</ref><ref name="Richens"/> It was introduced to New England in the 18th century,<ref>{{cite book |last=Browne |first=Daniel Jay |date=1851 |title=The Trees of America |publisher=Harper & Brothers |place=New York |page=481 |url=https://archive.org/stream/treesofamerican00brow#page/490/mode/2up }}</ref> and in the 19th century to Canada (as ''U. montana'' at the [[Dominion Arboretum]], [[Ottawa]]),<ref name = Ottawa1899>{{Cite book |last1=Saunders |first1=William |last2=Macoun |first2=William Tyrrell |url=https://archive.org/stream/bulletinissues00ottogoog#page/n80/mode/2up/ |title=Catalogue of the trees and shrubs in the arboretum and botanic gardens at the central experimental farm |year=1899 |edition=2 |pages=74–75 |publisher=Ottawa }}</ref> where a few old specimens survive,<ref>[https://canadiantreetours.org/species-pages/Scotch_elm.html Non-cultivar Scots elm in Toronto; canadiantreetours.org]</ref> and to Australia.<ref>Spencer, Roger, ed., ''Horticultural Flora of South-Eastern Australia'', Vol. 2 (Sydney, 1995), ''Ulmus'', p. 103-118 [https://books.google.com/books?id=jLabuEqJNNsC&dq=Horticultural+Flora+Of+South-+Eastern+Australia+ulmus&pg=PA105]</ref>

==Uses==

===Lumber===
Wych elm wood is prized by craftsmen for its colouring, its striking grain, its 'partridge-breast' or 'catspaw' markings, and when worked, its occasional iridescent greenish sheen or 'bloom'. The bosses on old trees produce the characteristic fissures and markings of 'burr elm' wood.<ref>Coleman, Max, ed., Wych Elm (Royal Botanic Garden publications, Edinburgh, 2009)</ref> Bosses fringed with shoots are burrs, whereas unfringed bosses are burls.{{citation needed|date=June 2025}}

===Medicine===
[[File:Ulmus campestris-Dijon.png|thumb|Medical properties of Ulmus campestris, Dijon, 1783]]
In 18th century France, the inner bark of ''Ulmus glabra'', ''orme pyramidale'', had a brief reputation as a [[panacea]];<ref>Simon Morelot, ''Cours élémentaire d'histoire naturelle pharmaceutique...'', 1800, [https://books.google.com/books?id=9JUT4F0xFaYC&pg=PA349 p. 349] "the elm, pompously named ''pyramidal''...it had an ephemeral reputation"</ref><ref name="gdb">Georges Dujardin-Beaumetz, ''Formulaire pratique de thérapeutique et de pharmacologie'', 1893, [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_L_6gFIvUKCcC/page/n706 p. 260]</ref>
"it was taken as a powder, as an extract, as an elixir, even in baths. It was good for the nerves, the chest, the stomach — what can I say? — it was a true panacea."<ref name="levis">Gaston de Lévis, ''Souvenirs et portraits, 1780-1789'', 1813, [https://books.google.com/books?id=bxXZmvs_15gC&pg=PA240 p. 240]</ref> It was this so-called "pyramidal elm bark" about which [[Michel-Philippe Bouvart]] famously quipped "Take it, Madame... and hurry up while it [still] cures."<ref name="levis"/> It still appeared in a pharmacopeia of 1893.<ref name="gdb"/>

==Notable trees==
[[File:ID 1481 Bergulme 001.jpg|thumb|Ancient ''U. glabra'' in [[Styria]], Austria]]
Possibly the oldest wych elm in Europe grew at [[Beauly Priory]] in [[Inverness-shire]], Scotland; the tree succumbed to Dutch elm disease in 2022 and collapsed the following year. The priory was founded circa 1230, the tree already in existence.<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-highlands-islands-64176914 'Europe's oldest' wych elm tree falls down in Beauly Priory]</ref>

The UK Champion listed in [[The Tree Register|the Tree Register of the British Isles]] was at [[Brahan Castle|Brahan]] in the [[Scottish Highlands]]<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070316002233/http://www.forestry.gov.uk/forestry/INFD-6UFDYA The Brahan Elm, forestry.gov.uk]</ref> (died 2021<ref name ="RBGE36814">[https://stories.rbge.org.uk/archives/36814 Coleman, Max, 'Wake-up call to climate change'; Botanics Stories, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, 2022]</ref>); it had a girth of 703 cm (2.23 m DBH) and a height of 24 m.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.woodland-trust.org.uk/ancient-tree-forum/future.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051109021605/http://www.woodland-trust.org.uk/ancient-tree-forum/future.pdf |archive-date=9 November 2005 |title=The Woodland Trust |access-date=2 November 2007 |url-status=live }}</ref> Possibly the oldest specimen in England was found in 2018 in a field north of [[Hopton Castle]] in Shropshire. Coppiced long ago, its bole girth measured 6.3 m in 2018. The oldest specimen in [[Edinburgh]] is believed to be the tree (girth 5.2 m) in the former grounds of [[Duddingston House]], now Duddingston Golf Course.<ref>CEC information; tree may be seen on Google Streetview, beside Cavalry Park Drive, E. of Holy Rood High School.</ref> Other notable specimens in Edinburgh are to be found in Learmonth Gardens and [[The Meadows (park)|The Meadows]].<ref>Edinburgh Wych-elm photographs [http://www.fombl.org.uk/tr_Wych_elm_1.html] [http://www.fombl.org.uk/tr_Wych_elm_2.html]</ref>

In Europe, a large tree planted in 1620 grows at Bergemolo, 5 km south of [[Demonte]] in [[Piedmont]], Italy (bole-girth 6.2 m, 2.0 m DBH, height 26 m., 2008).<ref name="patriarchinatura.it">Association of Nature Patriarchs in Italy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20160617214812/http://www.patriarchinatura.it/contenuti/it/patriarchi_regione/piemonte.php Piemonte - Olmo di Bergemolo], access-date: 23 November 2016</ref><ref name = "Bergemolo">{{cite web |url=https://www.google.co.uk/maps/@44.2952739,7.2854889,3a,90y,354.01h,119.16t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sEkU0qTaS1t1B9tSkt-9CEQ!2e0!7i13312!8i6656 |title=Olmo di Bergemolo, Piedmont Google Maps |work=Google.co.uk |access-date=7 February 2017 }}</ref> Other ancient specimens grow at Styria, in Austria, and at Grenzhammer, Germany (see Gallery).

==In literature==
[[E. M. Forster]] cites a particular wych elm, one that grew at his childhood home of Rooks Nest, [[Stevenage]], [[Hertfordshire]], 16 times in his novel ''[[Howards End]]''. This tree overhangs the house of the title and is said to have a "...girth that a dozen men could not have spanned..." Forster describes the tree as "...a comrade, bending over the house, strength and adventure in its roots." The wych elm of the novel had pigs' teeth embedded in the trunk by country people long ago and it was said that chewing some of the bark could cure toothache. In keeping with the novel's epigraph, "Only connect...", the wych elm may be seen by some as a symbol of the connection of humans to the earth. Margaret Schlegel, the novel's protagonist, fears that any "....westerly gale might blow the wych elm down and bring the end of all things..." The tree is changed to a chestnut in the 1991 film adaptation of ''[[Howards End (film)|Howards End]]''.

[[Ulmus 'Exoniensis'|'Exoniensis', Exeter Elm]], has traditionally been classified as a form of ''U. glabra''.

==Hybrids and hybrid cultivars==
''U. glabra'' hybridises naturally with ''[[U. minor|U. minor]]'', producing elms of the ''[[Ulmus × hollandica]]'' group, from which have arisen a number of cultivars:
{{#section:List of elm cultivars, hybrids and hybrid cultivars|Ulmus_x_hollandica_cultivars}}
However, hybrids of ''U. glabra'' and ''[[Ulmus pumila|U. pumila]]'', the Siberian elm, have not been observed in the field and only achieved in the laboratory, though the ranges of the two species, the latter introduced by man, overlap in parts of Southern Europe, notably Spain.<ref name="Martín"/> A crossing in Russia of ''U. glabra'' and ''U. pumila'' produced the hybrid named ''[[Ulmus × arbuscula]]''; a similar crossing was cloned ('FL025') by the Istituto per la Protezione delle Piante (IPP), Florence, as part of the Italian elm breeding programme circa 2000.

Hybrids with ''U. glabra'' in their ancestry have featured strongly in recent artificial hybridisation experiments in Europe, notably at [[Wageningen]] in the [[Netherlands]], and a number of hybrid cultivars have been commercially released since 1960.<ref name=Green>{{cite journal |last=Green |first=Peter Shaw |author-link=Peter Shaw Green |date=1964 |title=Registration of cultivar names in Ulmus |url=https://archive.org/stream/arnoldiaarno_21#page/40/mode/2up/ |journal=Arnoldia |volume=24 |pages=41–80 |number=6–8 |publisher=[[Arnold Arboretum]], [[Harvard University]] |doi=10.5962/p.249479 |access-date=16 February 2017 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The earlier trees were raised in response to the initial Dutch elm disease pandemic that afflicted Europe after the [[First World War]], and were to prove vulnerable to the much more virulent strain of the disease that arrived in the late 1960s. However, further research eventually produced several trees effectively immune to disease, which were released after 1989.<ref name=Heybroek,2>{{cite book |last1=Heybroek |first1=H.M. |editor1-last=Sticklen |editor1-first=Mariam B. |editor2-last=Sherald |editor2-first=James L. |title=Dutch Elm Disease Research |date=1993 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York, USA |pages=16–25 |access-date=26 October 2017 |chapter=The Dutch Elm Breeding Program |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=avvxBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA16 |isbn=978-1-4615-6874-2 }}</ref>
*[[Ulmus 'Arno'|Arno]], [[Ulmus 'Clusius'|Clusius]], [[Ulmus 'Columella'|Columella]], [[Ulmus 'Commelin'|Commelin]], [[Ulmus 'Den Haag'|Den Haag]], [[Ulmus 'Dodoens'|Dodoens]], [[Ulmus 'Groeneveld'|Groeneveld]], [[Ulmus 'Homestead'|Homestead]], [[Ulmus 'Lobel'|Lobel]], [[Ulmus 'Nanguen' = Lutece|Nanguen = {{tdes|Lutèce|caps}}]], [[Ulmus × hollandica 'Pioneer'|Pioneer]], [[Ulmus 'Plinio'|Plinio]], [[Ulmus 'Regal'|Regal]], [[Ulmus 'San Zanobi'|San Zanobi]], [[Ulmus 'Urban'|Urban]], [[Ulmus 'Wanoux' = Vada|Wanoux = {{tdes|Vada|caps}}]].
